messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 49-year-old architect who came to treatment after more than a year of trying to contain a reaction he could neither explain clearly nor outrun. He is married and still working, but he described moving through most days as if he were “bracing” for something. The trauma began when he witnessed a violent assault at close range outside a construction site he was visiting for work. He had stepped out near the service entrance at the end of a meeting, and the scene unfolded with sudden, shocking force: shouting, the unmistakable sound of bodies colliding, and the metallic, sour smell around the loading area mixing with what he later only called “that smell.” He remembers freezing as another man was beaten. What has stayed with him most is not a clean story but fragments with too much immediacy and too little order. He knows what happened, but when he tries to describe it he loses words, goes silent, and says the pieces come “all at once” rather than in sequence.

In the weeks afterward, David found that reminders reached him before he had time to think. News footage showing violence, a confrontation on the street, even a smell at a job site that resembled the odor from that loading area could bring on a wave of nausea and the immediate sense that the event was happening again. At those moments the memory did not feel like something from the past. He would be back there in his body, disoriented, unable to place what came first and what came next. Because these reminders landed so abruptly, he began entering conference rooms, restaurants, and client buildings already on guard. He would position himself with his back to a wall, scan for exits the moment he walked in, and jolt hard at ordinary noises, as if his body had learned that any setting could turn without warning.

As he tried to make sense of his reaction, David had come to believe there was something about him that had allowed the event to happen in front of him. He did not say this logically; he knew he had not caused the assault. But he felt marked by some personal failing, as if he lacked whatever other men have that lets them stop bad things. What frightened him most was the conviction that he could not prevent terrible events and would not see them coming. That belief sharpened his vigilance everywhere. In his office he now chooses the chair that lets him see the door and the whole room, and during site visits he automatically maps exit routes before he can focus on the plans in front of him.

Those same beliefs also seemed to make the world fill with reminders. Because he was certain that danger could break through anywhere and that he would again be helpless, signs of possible violence pulled his attention immediately: raised voices on the sidewalk, rough joking between contractors, footage playing on a waiting room television. Smells registered too quickly and too intensely. He noticed them, then his stomach turned, and the whole environment took on the charge of a warning. His wife has told him that other people seem able to let these things pass, but David feels set apart from them, as though he is living in a world where threat is always closer than anyone else understands.

Once his body goes on alert, the memories become even harder to keep in the past. If he is already scanning a room, tracking exits, and sitting rigidly with his back protected, any abrupt sound or movement can tip him into reliving. He then struggles even more to describe what happened, because the memory arrives as sensation and alarm rather than a coherent account. He leaves meetings remembering only flashes. On several occasions at work, after hearing shouting on a nearby floor or catching a related smell near building materials, he became so jumpy and nauseated that he had to step out, then found himself replaying the assault in fragments for the rest of the day.

Over time the vigilance has narrowed his life and fed the problem it is meant to solve. Because he is constantly checking rooms and monitoring other people, he is primed to notice exactly the kinds of cues that set him off. Each new startle, each scan for exits, each effort to stay positioned against a wall seems to confirm that danger is near, and the reminders come faster. At home he sits in restaurants only if he can face the entrance; at work he avoids parts of active sites where smells are strong or tempers run high. Colleagues have noticed he is more distracted during presentations, and his wife says he is physically present but far away.

He sought help after a client meeting in which a loud argument broke out in the hallway outside the conference room. David felt nauseated immediately, began searching for the exits before anyone else had even paused, and then lost the thread of where he was, caught in the sense that the assault was happening again. He was shaken by how quickly he could disappear from the present and by how impossible it still felt to put the original event into words. What he fears most is that this means he will never be able to trust himself in the world again; what he hopes, cautiously, is that he might learn how to be in a room without feeling he has to survive it.
